# How to Create AI-Generated Music for YouTube Videos in 2026

YouTubers hit the same wall eventually: the video is cut, and the music is wrong. Stock libraries return tracks everyone has heard, hiring a composer is out of budget for a weekly upload, and a wrong music choice can quietly cost watch time. AI music generation fixes the supply problem in minutes, which shifts the real work to three things you have to get right: prompting well, matching the track to your edit, and understanding what license you actually have. This guide walks the process in order.

## Step 1: Generate the track

[[link:/tools/1397|Suno]] creates complete songs with vocals and instruments from text prompts in seconds, and its strength for YouTube is full arrangements with a clear mood you can describe in plain language. If you want something more instrumental and controllable, [[link:/tools/1398|Udio]] generates high-quality songs and compositions across genres with prompts covering style, mood, and instrumentation. Both are Freemium. Be realistic about the failure modes: Suno tracks can sound generic without careful prompt refinement, and its free usage is limited while commercial terms should be checked. Udio's output quality varies and prompts may need several attempts, and its free quota is limited compared with paid plans. Budget for generating five candidates and using one.

## Step 2: Match the music to your edit

A generated track almost never fits a cut on the first try. [[link:/tools/69|Soundraw]] generates royalty-free instrumental music from parameters like mood, genre, and track length, and its differentiator is section editing: you can rearrange song sections so the music hits your edit points. That matters more than sound quality for retention. [[link:/tools/71|Beatoven]] composes background music matched to a video's mood and scene length, letting you adjust per scene, which suits videos with mood shifts like tutorials that turn into demos. Soundraw's limits: some regions require a VPN, and its focus is instrumental with no generated vocals. Beatoven's: access issues without a VPN in some regions, and output quality is best for backgrounds, not standalone listening.

## Step 3: Alternatives for different needs

[[link:/tools/1399|Mubert]] generates royalty-free tracks matched to mood, genre, and length, built for creators who need background music that will not trip copyright claims. Generated music can feel generic next to a composed score, and fine control over arrangement and instrumentation is limited. [[link:/tools/1339|Boomy]] generates full tracks in minutes and can publish songs directly to streaming platforms, but results can sound formulaic or synthetic, and fine control over instruments is limited. [[link:/tools/1566|Lyria]] is Google DeepMind's music model, producing structured tracks with verse and chorus sections plus timestamp-based control and SynthID watermarking on all generated audio. It requires access through Google AI Studio, the Gemini app, or the API, and generated music still benefits from human mixing and mastering.

## Step 4: Polish before upload

[[link:/tools/1427|LANDR]] combines AI mastering with music distribution, turning a rough mix into a stream-ready master adjusted for streaming loudness targets. Two honest limits: AI mastering cannot fully replace an engineer for tricky mixes, and preset-based results may sound similar across a catalog. For a YouTube upload, that is usually fine, because the goal is a track that sits under voice without pumping. Run the master, then check it on phone speakers, because that is where most of your audience listens.

## Licensing: the part creators skip

This is where AI music goes wrong. Each tool's commercial terms differ, and a track that is fine for a personal video may not be fine for a monetized channel. Suno's own data flags that commercial terms should be checked. Mubert's royalty-free output avoids copyright claims on monetized platforms, but read the current terms for your plan. Lyria watermarks all generated audio with SynthID, which is transparency you should be aware of, not a defect. Before your first monetized upload, read the license page of whichever tool you used and keep a record of it.

## How to choose between them

If you want full songs with vocals and are willing to curate, Suno. If you need instrumental beds that follow your edit, Soundraw or Beatoven, where section editing is the feature that matters. If you need quick royalty-free tracks with the least fuss, Mubert. If you want structured output with modern model quality and API access, Lyria. If you want to also release tracks to streaming services, Boomy, accepting the formulaic risk. All are Freemium, so the deciding factor should be output fit for your genre, not brand.

## A workflow that chains them

The full chain for a weekly channel: describe the mood in a prompt, generate candidates with Suno or Udio, pick the best, import into Soundraw or Beatoven and rearrange sections to hit your edit points, drop it under the cut, master with LANDR, then export and upload with a note of which tool generated it and under which license. Total time once you have a workflow: under an hour for music that used to take days of library browsing.

## Common mistakes

First, uploading with the license question unanswered; monetization claims are the fastest way to learn. Second, picking music louder than your voice, which hurts retention more than any other mix mistake. Third, letting a generated vocal track bury narration; prompt for instrumental unless vocals are the point. Fourth, reusing the same generated track across every video until viewers associate it with your channel in the wrong way. And fifth, skipping the edit-match step, which is where generated music usually fails.

## FAQ

**Is AI music copyright-free?** Tools generate royalty-free audio under their terms, but the terms differ per tool and plan, so check before monetizing.

**Can I use Suno tracks on a monetized channel?** Suno's documentation says commercial terms should be checked, so verify your plan's terms before your first monetized upload.

**Which tool fits music to my edit?** Soundraw and Beatoven both support section-level adjustment, which is what edit-matching actually requires.

**Do I need to master AI tracks?** A light master with LANDR or similar helps tracks sit consistently under voice, and preset-based results are fine for background use.

Generate, curate, match, master, and document the license. Do those five things and AI music stops being a risk and becomes the easiest part of your upload.
tldr: Generate a track with Suno or Mubert, match its structure to your edit with Soundraw or Beatoven, master it with LANDR, and check each tool's commercial terms before monetizing. Free tiers cover the whole first pass.
